newsitem.title: JAPAN: Pioneer back on recovery path with upbeat profits.
newsitem.headline: Pioneer back on recovery path with upbeat profits.

text.p: Japanese audio-visual equipment maker Pioneer Electronic Corp is back on a recovery track, pulling itself out of a rut created by sluggish sales of its mainstay laser disc players.

On Monday, Pioneer announced strong profit growth for the April-June quarter of 1997, aided by a restructuring programme, steady gains in sales of its car navigation systems and a pick-up in digital video disc (DVD) players.

Pioneer's group net profits surged 27.5 percent to 1.03 billion yen ($8.8 million) in the first quarter of fiscal year 1997/98. The company also reported 953 million yen ($8.14 million) in operating profits, a complete reversal from a 1.11 billion yen ($9.4 million) loss a year ago. The profits were largely in line with market expectations.

"Profitability in the car electronics division improved, helping to raise operating profits as a whole," said a Pioneer spokesman. "We expect higher sales of DVD players to help make up for shrinking sales of LDs (laser discs) this year."

Pioneer executive vice president Masaaki Sono told a news conference that first quarter sales were buoyed by the yen's decline against the dollar, which raised group sales by 5.48 billion yen ($46.8 million).

Sales of its laser discs have sharply declined since DVDs, with far greater capacity than conventional video cassettes, compact discs and laser discs, made their debut on the global market early this year.
Sales of its on-line Karaoke sing-along system that uses laser discs also sagged, amid intensified competition from Sony Corp and other newcomers.
Sono said Pioneer expects to sell 20 billion yen ($170 million) worth of laser disc products in 1997/98, down from 23 billion yen ($196 million) in the prior year.

He added that Pioneer will meet its group net profit forecast for the 1997/98 year ending March 31 of eight billion to nine billion yen ($68.3 to $76.9 million), assuming an average dollar/yen rate for the year of 117 yen per dollar.

Analysts said Pioneer stands to benefit more than other Japanese electronics makers from sales of DVD players, whose popularity is still limited due to a dearth of video titles and other pre-recorded content available in the DVD format.

"Pioneer, which focuses on DVD-LD compatible players, is well-positioned in the sales race because consumers can also play conventional laser discs on Pioneer's machines," said Yoshiharu Izumi, an analyst at UBS Securities.
Pioneer currently has nearly half of the domestic DVD market and 20 percent of the U.S. market, Izumi said.

Rising sales of DVD players will start contributing to Pioneer's profits after July, while sales of plasma panels will begin adding to the company's bottom line next year, said Masaru Koshida, an analyst at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.
Pioneer last year reduced its workforce by 998, from an original total of 7,300, through a restructuring programme that included an early-retirement scheme. ($1=117 yen)
